verses.translation_literal: Dwelling in the shelter of Most High, in the shadow of Shaddai he will lodge.
verses.translation_dramatic: Whoever sits down in the hidden place of the Most High, whoever beds down for the night in the long shade of the Almighty, that one is kept.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens without a name, without a title, without a speaker: just a participle, 'dwelling', hanging in the air like a door left open. Say it quietly. The KJV's 'secret place' is not wrong, but it sounds like a hidden room in an English house; seter is a covering, a hiding-place, the cover under which you vanish from an enemy, and it is parallel to 'shadow' in the second line. Shade is not a pleasant extra in the ancient Near East; in a land of scorching sun and open country it is the difference between a day you survive and one you do not.

The two verbs matter. 'Dwelling' (yoshev) is to sit, to settle; 'lodge' (yitlonan) is the verb for spending the night, and the form here stresses repeated, settled staying. So the first line is the settled resident, the second the traveler who spends the night: both stay under the same cover. The KJV's 'shall abide' flattens that. Two divine titles are paired: Elyon, 'Most High', and Shaddai, 'Almighty' (the KJV and Rashi, who glosses it as 'strength', make it a title of power). Both are old, pre-Mosaic titles, and the poet uses them instead of the covenant name, saving YHWH for v.2.

philological_notes.note: To lodge, to spend the night. The stem here suggests continuing or habitual lodging; Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'continuance', citing Isa 1:21 ('righteousness lodged in it'). 'Abide' in the KJV loses the picture of a night's rest.
A covering or hiding-place: what conceals you, not a 'secret' in the sense of knowledge. It is the shelter that protects by hiding.

verses.translation_literal: I say to YHWH, "My refuge and my stronghold, my God, I trust in him."
verses.translation_dramatic: I say it to the LORD, and I say it plainly: my refuge, my fortress, my God; in him I put my whole weight.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice drops from description to confession, and the actor should feel the turn: after the impersonal 'whoever' of v.1 comes an 'I'. Who is speaking is a real question. Rashi hears the psalmist modeling the words for everyone; Ibn Ezra, Radak, Malbim and Meiri hear a speaker addressing the listener 'on behalf of' the LORD, with 'I say to you for the sake of the LORD that he is my refuge', and that is why v.3 turns to 'you'. The Hebrew gives no marker, so keep the ambiguity alive in the delivery: it is a testimony that becomes an address.

Two military images carry the line. Machseh, 'refuge', is a place to flee for cover; metzudah, 'stronghold', is a mountain fortress, the kind built on cliffs where the Judean hills offer them. The KJV's 'fortress' is fine, but it breaks the line by inserting 'He is' and moving 'my God' after a colon, so the staccato run of nouns is lost: refuge, stronghold, God, trust. Here the divine name appears for the first time, YHWH, after two titles in v.1.

philological_notes.note: A stronghold, a fortified height; Metzudat Zion glosses it as a strong fortification. The same noun can mean a net or snare (from the root 'hunt'), which gives an ironic echo against 'snare' in the next verse.

'I say to YHWH', or, as Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David and Malbim read the lamed, 'I say, for the sake of YHWH'. The plain sense is addressed to God; the commentators' reading explains the shift to 'you' in v.3.

verses.translation_literal: For he, he will deliver you from the snare of a fowler, from a plague of ruin.
verses.translation_dramatic: For he himself will pull you free, out of the fowler's snare, out of the plague that brings ruin.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'for' (ki) is the argument: here is the reason for the trust of v.2, spoken now to 'you'. The pronoun 'he' is stated outright before the verb, which the Hebrew does only for stress: he, and no one else. Deliver it with weight on that word.

The first danger is a bird-trap. Yaqush is a man who sets nets for birds; pach is the spring-net or snare. The image is cunning and hidden: the victim does not see the trap until it closes. That sets up the bird imagery of v.4, where the one rescued from the fowler is the bird sheltered under wings. The second danger is deber, 'plague' or pestilence, here with hawwot, 'ruin' or 'destruction', not the KJV's 'noisome', an old word for harmful that comes from a guess at the root that modern lexicons do not follow. Radak glosses hawwot simply as 'breaking, ruin'. The pairing is deliberate: a human enemy who plots (the fowler) and a calamity that no one plots (the plague).

philological_notes.note: 'Ruin', 'destruction' (plural, an intensive). Metzudat Zion and Radak gloss it as breaking or ruin, citing Ezek 7:26 ('ruin upon ruin'). KJV 'noisome' is not supported by this sense.
A fowler, the one who sets a snare (Radak: an adjective in place of a participle, 'the one who ensnares'). Metzudat Zion links it to the word for a trap, moqesh.

verses.translation_literal: With his pinion he will cover for you, and under his wings you will take refuge; a shield and an encircling shield [is] his faithfulness.
verses.translation_dramatic: He will spread his pinion over you, and beneath his wings you will find your hiding place. His faithfulness is a shield, and more than a shield: a ring of defence drawn all the way around you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice stays tender, and the picture is a bird over her young, not a warrior in armour. Deut 32:11 uses the same rare word for the eagle's pinion (Ibn Ezra hears that echo: God stirs his nest like an eagle), so an Israelite audience already knew the image: a protector who is large, near and living. Then the metaphor changes without warning, from feathers to metalwork, and the actor should let that jolt show: the refuge that felt soft turns out to be armed.

The KJV 'trust' for תֶּחְסֶה loses the physical picture: the verb means to take refuge, to run under cover, and it is the word for chicks under wings. 'His truth' for אֱמֶת is also thin; the word is reliability, faithfulness that holds weight, which is why a shield can stand for it. The KJV's 'buckler' picks a particular kind of shield for a word that occurs only here. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat Zion all derive סֹחֵרָה from סחור סחור, 'round and round': a defence that goes around the whole person, where the צִנָּה (the large shield) covers the front. Meiri says the same: one covers the front only, the other all sides. The Targum renders it 'round' (עגילא). So play it as a shield plus a wall that wraps around, not as two named items of kit.

philological_notes.note: 'Pinion', the long wing feather or wing. Rare: Deut 32:11 (the eagle) and Job 39:13. Malbim separates אֵבֶר, the wing as a limb, from כָּנָף, the spread feathers.
Occurs only here. Read as 'encircling' from סחר 'go around'; the commentators take it as a shield that surrounds the body, not as a named piece of armour.
From אֱמֶת, firmness, reliability; here God's faithfulness to his promise. Radak and Metzudat David read it as the truth of his promise.

verses.translation_literal: Not you will fear from the dread of night, from an arrow [that] flies by day.
verses.translation_dramatic: You will not shrink from the terror of the night, nor from the arrow that flies in the open light of day.
verses.directors_commentary:
Night and day are a merism: no hour of the clock is left uncovered, and the next verse adds darkness and noon. Night is when the town sleeps and the traveller or the lone shepherd is alone; Radak says it is the loneliness of night that makes a person dread. The actor should not play bravado: the promise is made to someone who has felt exactly this fear.

The KJV's 'afraid for the terror' is archaic; the Hebrew has מִן, 'afraid from'. Notice the verb of the arrow, יָעוּף, 'it flies': it is the verb for birds, and it follows hard on the wings of verse 4. The danger flies; the protector also has wings.

What the terror and the arrow are is old debate. Rashi reads the day arrow as a flying demon, shooting like an arrow. The Targum goes further: the night terror is the dread of demons that walk by night, and the day arrow is the arrow of the angel of death, shot by day. Radak and Meiri read both as ordinary perils, the sudden blows of circumstance and the surprise of an ambush.

philological_notes.note: 'Dread of night': the fear itself, not the thing feared. The Targum places demons in it; Radak and Meiri think of the isolation of the night and of ambush.
'An arrow [that] flies': the verb is the one used for birds. Rashi hears a flying demon; Radak and Meiri an arrow or a swift blow.

verses.translation_literal: From a plague [that] in the darkness walks, from destruction [that] devastates at noon.
verses.translation_dramatic: Nor at the plague that goes walking through the darkness, nor at the destruction that lays waste at high noon.
verses.directors_commentary:
The list continues in the same pairing of dark and light, but now both dangers are personified: the plague walks, the destruction devastates. Deber has been 'plague' since v.3; qetev is a rarer word, 'cutting off', as Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion say, with a parallel in Hos 13:14. Neither is a precise disease: they are the names of what kills in bulk.

But the ancient audience heard more in the line. Rashi, citing the Talmud (Pesachim 111b), and the Aramaic Targum both read deber and qetev as names of demons, one that harms by night and one at noon; the noon demon was a known idea, and the Septuagint has the 'noonday demon' here. Whether or not the poet meant demons, the actor should play the dangers as things with intent, not weather. Ibn Ezra and Meiri give the natural reading: the plague comes with winter cold at night, the 'destruction' with the summer heat at noon. Noon is the hour of exposure, when the heat is at its worst, a time when work stops and a man alone is most vulnerable. The KJV's 'wasteth' is a fair sense of yashud; its 'walketh in darkness' is literal.

philological_notes.note: 'Cutting off', destruction. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion link it to Hos 13:14 ('O Death, I will be your qetev'). Rashi and the rabbinic tradition take it as a demon's name.
'Devastates', 'lays waste', from the root for plunder and ruin. Rashi cites Hos 10:2 for the sense; Meiri notes the alternative link to the word for demons (shedim).

verses.translation_literal: There will fall from your side a thousand, and a myriad from your right hand; to you it will not draw near.
verses.translation_dramatic: A thousand will go down beside you, ten thousand at your right hand, and it will not come near you.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the psalm: the promise is not that nothing happens, but that the speaker is standing in the middle of it. The ranks fall on both sides, and the listener walks through untouched. Play it quietly. A shout turns it into a boast; it is awe.

The numbers climb as in the old war songs: a thousand, then a myriad (רְבָבָה, ten thousand), as in 'Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands'. Meiri adds that the right hand, the side of honour, takes the larger number. The Hebrew does not say 'but' before the last clause, as the KJV does: the sentences simply stand side by side, which sounds harsher. The 'it' that will not come near is unnamed: the arrow, the plague or death itself. 'Nigh' is archaic for 'near'.

On the verb: Rashi takes יִפֹּל as 'encamp', as in Gen 25:18, 'he fell [settled] over against all his brothers', and reads a thousand demons camped at the left. That sense of 'fall' is attested, but here the plain sense, with 'it will not come near you', is falling dead, and Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David and Malbim all read it so, whether in war or in plague. The Targum has a condition in it: they fall 'when you remember the name of the Holy One'.

philological_notes.note: 'It will fall.' The plain sense is falling dead in battle or plague. Rashi reads 'encamp' as in Gen 25:18, which is a real sense of the verb but less natural beside 'it will not come near you'.
A myriad, ten thousand, the largest round number; the pair thousand and myriad is a stock merism for a vast multitude. Meiri says the right hand's larger number reflects its greater honour.

verses.translation_literal: Only with your eyes you will look, and the retribution of wicked [people] you will see.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have only to look with your own eyes, and you will watch the wicked repaid.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'only' (raq) is a limit: the protected one is a witness, nothing more. You will look; it will not touch you. The line makes the rescue an act of observation, which is why the verbs are about seeing: tabbit, 'look', and tir'eh, 'see', a doubled verb for the eyes, which the KJV renders as one 'behold and see'.

Shillumat is the key word: 'recompense', 'repayment', from the root for 'pay in full' and 'make whole' (shalem). The wicked get what they paid for; the word has the sound of a bill settled. The KJV's 'reward' sounds like a prize, which is the opposite of what the poet means here. Metzudat David and Radak take the verse plainly: the fallen of v.7 are the wicked, and the safe one sees their end. Malbim finds a moral argument: the sight of the fallen shows that divine justice is real. Rashi's gloss is 'destruction' for shillumat, with the question 'and why?' left for the next verse to answer.

philological_notes.note: 'Repayment', 'retribution', a payment in full. It is the Hebrew root of 'peace' and 'wholeness' used here for an account settled, so 'reward' (KJV) misleads.

verses.translation_literal: For you, YHWH, [are] my refuge; Most High you have made your dwelling.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you, LORD, are my refuge; and you have made the Most High your dwelling-place.
verses.directors_commentary:
A new voice breaks in, and the verse is hard on purpose. The speaker of v.2 says 'You, YHWH, are my refuge', and the second voice answers with 'you have made the Most High your dwelling'. The accents of the Hebrew divide the verse there: one clause addressed to YHWH, one to the listener. ASV and YLT follow this; the KJV and Webster fuse them into 'thou hast made the LORD, which is my refuge, even the Most High, thy habitation', which makes the divine name the object of 'made' and turns a speaker's cry into a subordinate clause.

The Rabbinic commentators fill in the speech: Rashi says it is brief ('you said: the LORD is my refuge'), Radak and Ibn Ezra take it as the poet speaking to the faithful. Me'onah is a dwelling, a home, and it echoes v.1 with its 'dwelling' and 'shelter', and it is the word used of God's own dwelling and of lairs. The 'you' is chosen: you set your home there, so the harm cannot enter. Malbim puts it vividly: you live in a place that harm cannot reach.

philological_notes.note: 'Your dwelling-place', a home or lair. Metzudat Zion glosses it as a dwelling; Metzudat David sees trust in God like a person trusting the house that keeps off rain and flood.
'You have made / set': a deliberate act of placing. The perfect tense marks the choice as done and settled.

verses.translation_literal: No harm will be allowed to happen to you, and plague will not draw near in your tent.
verses.translation_dramatic: No harm will be sent your way, and no plague will come close to the tent where you live.
verses.directors_commentary:
The promise now moves from the field to the home, from the battle line to the tent flap. The tent (ohel) is the household of an ancient family: the herdsman, his wife, his children, his animals. Radak spells it out: not to you, your wife or your sons. This is a setting of nomads and farmers, not of a city, and the KJV's 'dwelling' loses the picture of a cloth roof that a plague passes over.

The verb te'unneh is rare and strange. It is a passive form of a root that means 'to cause to happen', as in Ex 21:13, 'God caused it to happen into his hand'. So the sense is 'harm will not be allowed to happen to you', as though harm needed permission. Malbim goes further: harm itself would not wish to touch you. The KJV's 'befall' gets the sense. The second line gives 'plague' (nega), a word that in Leviticus names the skin affection that makes a house or a person unclean; the plague that cannot come near is also the disease that marks you out.

philological_notes.note: A passive of the root 'to cause to happen, to let befall': 'will not be made to happen'. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion compare Ex 21:13, 'God let it happen into his hand'.
A blow, a stroke, and in Leviticus the name for a disease or mark that makes a person or dwelling unclean. Here 'plague'.

token_glosses.gloss: will it be allowed to happen

verses.translation_literal: For his angels he will command for you, to guard you in all your ways.
verses.translation_dramatic: For he will give his messengers their orders on your behalf: to guard you in every road you take.
verses.directors_commentary:
The reason for the safety is a command given in heaven, and the actors should hear the scene as a briefing: God issues orders to his messengers, and the subject of the orders is 'you'. Mal'akhim means 'messengers', and the same word is used for human envoys; 'angels' in the KJV is from the Greek, and the Hebrew word asks 'who is sending them and for what', which the verse answers.

The 'for you' (lakh) is not 'over you' as the KJV has it: Ibn Ezra and Radak read the lamed as 'for your sake', as in Gen 20:13 ('say of me, he is my brother'), an old idiom the Hebrew uses in v.2 as well. 'Charge over thee' is a paraphrase, though not a wrong one. The scope is 'all your ways', all the roads and journeys of a life, not only the dangers named so far; it is the widest promise in the psalm, and the speaker should open the voice here. Meiri sees it as the providence that arranges circumstances in your favour, not the hand of a bodyguard.

philological_notes.note: 'He will command for you': God gives the messengers their orders for your sake. Ibn Ezra and Radak take the lamed as 'for you / on your behalf', as in Gen 20:13.
'His messengers'. The Hebrew word is an office, 'one sent', not a species; the KJV 'angels' fixes it as heavenly beings, which the context supports.

verses.translation_literal: On hands they will lift you, lest you strike on the stone your foot.
verses.translation_dramatic: They will carry you in their palms, so that your foot will never strike a stone.
verses.directors_commentary:
The most tender picture in the psalm, and the smallest danger: a loose stone on the path. After arrows, plagues and the fall of thousands, the final threat is a stubbed foot. That is the point. The guardians are so attentive that even the least harm is kept off, and they do it the way a parent carries a child over rough ground. Metzudat David and Meiri read it as a figure, not a literal flight; Malbim takes it further, with the angels afraid you might so much as bruise a toe.

The Hebrew is spare: 'on hands' (kappayim, the dual, a pair of palms), 'they will lift you' (yissa'unekha, the same verb as to carry a burden or a child), and a stubbed foot, with the verb tigof ('strike', also used of a plague or a defeat in battle, which sets the small stone beside the great blows of v.7). The KJV's 'dash' is stronger than the Hebrew, which is 'strike' or 'stub'; its 'bear thee up in their hands' is good. Rashi glosses it 'stumble' and adds an Old French word (written in Hebrew letters in the packet). Stones are real in the Judean hills, and every traveler knew their danger.

philological_notes.note: 'You strike', a blow, as in a foot against a stone; the root is also used of plague and military defeat (Metzudat Zion links it to Ex 21:22). Rashi glosses it 'stumble'.
'On palms': the dual of 'palm of the hand'. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'as if on palms'; Metzudat David takes it as a figure for the greatness of the protection.

verses.translation_literal: On a lion and a cobra you will tread; you will trample a young lion and a serpent.
verses.translation_dramatic: Upon the lion and the cobra you will set your foot; the young lion and the serpent you will trample down.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the gentle image of angels' hands, the picture turns: the one who was carried now walks over the beasts. Four creatures: two lions and two snakes, the killers of the open country and the ones underfoot, so that danger from above and from below is covered. The verbs are tread (דָּרַךְ, to step down on, as one treads a winepress or a bow) and trample (רָמַס). Say them with weight: this is a conqueror's gait.

The names are all different words, which English tends to blur. שַׁחַל is a poetic word for lion (Metzudat Zion: one of the names of the lion); כְּפִיר is the young lion, strong and in his prime (Metzudat Zion calls him an ארי בחור, a lion in his youth); פֶּתֶן is a cobra or asp, the snake of Deut 32:33 and Isa 11:8; תַּנִּין is a serpent, and elsewhere a sea monster. The KJV's 'adder' is a fair snake for peten, but 'dragon' is no longer what an English ear hears in תַּנִּין; the Hebrew is a big snake or sea creature, not a winged monster. 'Under feet' is simply archaic for 'underfoot'. Meiri and Malbim, each in his own way, take the beasts as figures for strong enemies, and Ibn Ezra and Radak as a promise that wild animals will do no harm even when walked on.

philological_notes.note: A poetic word for lion, used in parallel with other lion words (Job 4:10; 28:8). Metzudat Zion calls it one of the lion's names.
A cobra or asp, a venomous snake; a distinct word from תַּנִּין.
A serpent or a sea creature (as in Exod 7:9, the snake of Aaron's staff). Not a dragon in the later European sense.

verses.translation_literal: For in me he has desired, and I will deliver him; I will set him on high, for he has known my name.
verses.translation_dramatic: Because his heart has clung to me, I will bring him out safe. I will lift him beyond all reach, because he has known my name.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice changes. Until now someone has spoken about God; here the first person arrives with no 'thus says the LORD', and the actor should simply change the colour of the voice. That bare 'me' is the moment the whole psalm has been leading to. Ibn Ezra takes it as God addressing the angels about their charge; Radak and Meiri as God speaking of the faithful one, and Meiri notes that prophecy moves freely between 'he', 'you' and 'I'.

The KJV's 'set his love upon me' is a good English phrase, but it makes the verb sound mild. חָשַׁק is strong desire, being attached to someone; elsewhere it is used of Shechem longing for Dinah (Gen 34:8) and, with God as the subject, of the LORD's attachment to Israel (Deut 7:7) and to the fathers (Deut 10:15). Here it is turned around: a human being is the one who clings to God. The KJV also writes 'therefore will I deliver him', where the Hebrew has only 'and'; the reason is carried by 'for' (כִּי) at both ends of the verse. The two verbs of rescue are אֲפַלְּטֵהוּ, 'I will let him slip away safe' (the verb of an escape), and אֲשַׂגְּבֵהוּ, 'I will set him on high', out of reach; it is the verb behind מִשְׂגָּב, 'stronghold'.

'To know my name' is not to have heard it but to be in relationship with the one who bears it. In the ancient world a name was a person's reputation and access. Radak connects it to the four-letter divine name and to a close relationship with God.

philological_notes.note: To be attached to, to desire. Elsewhere: Shechem for Dinah (Gen 34:8); God for Israel (Deut 7:7) and for the fathers (Deut 10:15). Here a human is the subject: clinging to God. Meiri: it expresses an attachment that shuns everything else.
'I will set him on high', out of reach of danger; the root also gives מִשְׂגָּב, 'stronghold'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as strengthening.
'Has known my name': knowing in the sense of acquaintance and relationship. Radak links it to the divine name; Metzudat David reads it as knowing and revering the name.

token_glosses.gloss: I will set him on high

verses.translation_literal: He will call me and I will answer him; with him [am] I in trouble; I will rescue him and I will honor him.
verses.translation_dramatic: When he cries out to me, I will answer him. In the narrow place I am with him. I will pull him free, and I will give him honor.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the most tender verse of the oracle, and it should be played quietly after the thunder of the beasts. The sequence is four moves: he calls, I answer, I am with him, I rescue him and honor him. The centre is a three-word nominal clause, 'with him I, in trouble', with no verb at all, so that the presence of God is stated as a fact rather than a promise; the English versions all add 'will be' or 'am', and the KJV 'I will be with him' makes it a future event. Radak reads it as: the faithful man will not be afraid, for I am with him (Radak on Psalms 91:15). Meiri also finds here Isaiah 63:9, 'in all their trouble he was troubled' (Meiri on Psalms 91:15).

The word for trouble, tsarah, comes from a root meaning narrow, a tight place, the picture of a man in a gorge with no room to move. Chalatz is to draw out, to pull free, 'extraction and drawing out' in Metzudat Zion's phrase (on Psalms 91:15); the KJV's 'deliver' has already been used for palat in verse 14, so it hides that Hebrew has a different verb here. Kaved, 'honor', is 'make heavy': to give someone weight in the eyes of others. Radak says it is grace and honor in the eyes of all people (Radak on Psalms 91:15).

philological_notes.note: In trouble, in a tight place. The root means to bind or narrow, and the noun is the common word for distress.
To draw out, rescue; also to pull off a sandal or draw a weapon. Metzudat Zion glosses it as taking out and drawing.

verses.translation_literal: Length of days I will satisfy him, and I will let him look on my salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: Long years I will give him, until he is full of them. And my salvation, I will let him look upon it with his own eyes.
verses.directors_commentary:
The oracle closes on two promises, and the first is a feast: sava is to be sated, as a guest is full after a meal. Long life is not a number but a fullness; a man dies 'old and satisfied with days' in Genesis 25:8 and Job 42:17, and the actor should hold the word 'satisfy' as a man sitting back from a table. The KJV 'with long life will I satisfy him' is right, but its modern ring of 'enough' hides the ancient sense of abundance. Metzudat David reads it so: he will be full of days, because they are so many (Metzudat David on Psalms 91:16).

The last clause is the one the readers fought over. 'I will let him look on my salvation' has the verb ra'ah in the causative with the preposition be, 'let him gaze on', and the KJV's 'shew him' loses the pleasure of looking. What is the salvation? Ibn Ezra offers both the light of the divine presence and the days of the Messiah (Ibn Ezra on Psalms 91:16); Radak reads the world to come, or the resurrection when God saves Israel from exile (Radak on Psalms 91:16); Meiri thinks of the time of redemption (Meiri on Psalms 91:16). Metzudat David keeps it close to the page: in his days he will see with his own eyes the deliverance of the LORD (Metzudat David on Psalms 91:16). Play it open-ended, as the Hebrew leaves it.

philological_notes.note: 'Length of days', the Hebrew idiom for a long life, the reward of the righteous in Proverbs 3:2 and 3:16 and in the Torah's promise.

'On my salvation', with the preposition be after the verb 'see', meaning look on with satisfaction. The commentaries differ on what the salvation is: the divine light, the messianic days or the world to come.

token_glosses.gloss: and I will let him look
